### Primary Finding & Data-Grounded Hypothesis

In the Reproducibility Project: Psychology (`rpp`), **junior professors (defined as Assistant Professors in replication teams, `seniority.r`) account for 28.57% (10 out of 35, or ~28.6%) of successfully replicated studies**. 

If defined more broadly to include non-tenure/graduate research assistants (`Assistant Professor` + `Assistant`), the proportion rises to **45.71%** (16 out of 35). In contrast, among the original authors of replicated studies (`seniority.o`), junior professors account for **0.0%** (0 out of 35), as original authors were overwhelmingly senior faculty (85.7% Full Professors, 11.4% Associate Professors, and 2.9% Researchers).

**Data-Grounded Hypothesis:**
> In psychological science replications, junior professors (Assistant Professors) serve as the most senior replication investigator in approximately 28.6% of successfully replicated studies (and up to 32.3% in cleaned quality-controlled samples). Replication success is not hindered by junior seniority; in fact, replication teams led by junior professors replicate at a rate of 43.48% (10/23) compared to 33.78% (25/74) for teams led by other ranks, although this difference is not statistically significant ($\chi^2 = 0.36, p = 0.55$).

---

### Detailed Findings & Seniority Distribution

#### 1. Primary Analysis: RPP Replication Seniority (`seniority.r`)
Among all 97 Psychology replication studies in RPP, 35 studies successfully replicated (`replicated == 1`, $p \le 0.05$ with consistent effect direction) and 62 failed to replicate:

| Seniority Rank (`seniority.r`) | Replicated Count ($N=35$) | Replicated Proportion | Non-Replicated Count ($N=62$) | Non-Replicated Proportion |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Assistant Professor** | **10** | **28.57%** | 13 | 20.97% |
| **Professor** (Full) | 8 | 22.86% | 11 | 17.74% |
| **Associate Professor** | 7 | 20.00% | 17 | 27.42% |
| **Assistant** | 6 | 17.14% | 9 | 14.52% |
| **Researcher** | 4 | 11.43% | 12 | 19.35% |
| **Total** | **35** | **100.0%** | **62** | **100.0%** |

- **Strict Junior Professor definition (`Assistant Professor`)**: **28.57%** (10 / 35).
- **Broad Junior definition (`Assistant Professor` + `Assistant`)**: **45.71%** (16 / 35).

---

### Sensitivity & Robustness Checks

1. **Filtering by `drop == False`**:
   - 7 studies in RPP have `drop == True` (4 replicated, 3 non-replicated).
   - In the filtered dataset ($N = 31$ replicated studies), Assistant Professors represent **32.26%** (10 out of 31), Associate Professors 22.58% (7/31), Full Professors 19.35% (6/31), Assistants 19.35% (6/31), and Researchers 6.45% (2/31).

2. **Original Author Seniority (`seniority.o`) vs. Replication Author Seniority (`seniority.r`)**:
   - In the original studies of the 35 replicated psychology papers, **0.0%** (0 / 35) of most senior authors were Assistant Professors:
     - Full Professor: 30 (85.71%)
     - Associate Professor: 4 (11.43%)
     - Researcher: 1 (2.86%)
     - Assistant Professor: 0 (0.00%)
   - Across the entire RPP dataset ($N = 97$), no original papers were led by an Assistant Professor (83 Full Professors, 9 Associate Professors, 5 Researchers).

3. **Broader Scope of Psychology (RPP + Many Labs 1 & 3)**:
   - When including all studies in Cognitive and Social disciplines across RPP, Many Labs 1, and Many Labs 3:
     - Multi-lab replication leads are uniformly recorded as `Professor` in `seniority.r`.
     - At the unique / aggregated study level ($N = 52$ replicated psychology studies), junior professors account for **19.23%** (10 / 52).
     - At the unaggregated lab-site level ($N = 372$ replicated rows), junior professors account for **2.69%** (10 / 372).

payload.workflow: Filtered meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv for project == 'rpp' and replicated == 1; tabulated seniority.r and seniority.o; performed sensitivity analyses across drop filtering and multi-lab scopes; executed chi-squared independence test.
payload.hypothesis: In psychological science replications, junior professors (Assistant Professors) constitute approximately 28.6% of replication leads in successfully replicated studies (32.3% in quality-screened samples), showing that junior researchers actively lead successful replications at rates comparable to or slightly exceeding senior colleagues.
